claim: The posterior parietal cortex (PPC) contributes to the control of visually guided locomotor gait modifications by constructing an estimation of object location relative to body state.
source: We test the hypothesis that the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) contributes to the control of visually guided locomotor gait modifications by constructing an estimation of object location relative to body state, and in particular the changing gap between them.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis being tested in the study, supported by the experimental design and results presented.

claim: Neuronal activity was recorded from areas 5b and 7 of the PPC of cats walking on a treadmill and stepping over a moving obstacle.
source: To test this hypothesis, we recorded neuronal activity from areas 5b and 7 of the PPC of cats walking on a treadmill and stepping over a moving obstacle whose speed of advance was varied (slowed or accelerated with respect to the speed of the cat).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Distinct populations of neurons in the PPC, primarily in area 5b, signal distance-to-contact with the obstacle.
source: We found distinct populations of neurons in the PPC, primarily in area 5b, that signaled distance- or time-to-contact with the obstacle, regardless of which limb was the first to step over the obstacle.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: Distinct populations of neurons in the PPC, primarily in area 5b, signal time-to-contact with the obstacle.
source: We found distinct populations of neurons in the PPC, primarily in area 5b, that signaled distance- or time-to-contact with the obstacle, regardless of which limb was the first to step over the obstacle.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The neuronal populations that signal distance- or time-to-contact do so regardless of which limb is the first to step over the obstacle.
source: We found distinct populations of neurons in the PPC, primarily in area 5b, that signaled distance- or time-to-contact with the obstacle, regardless of which limb was the first to step over the obstacle.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the recorded neurons showing limb-independence.

claim: These cells are involved in a sensorimotor transformation whereby information on the location of an obstacle with respect to the body is used to initiate the gait modification.
source: We propose that these cells are involved in a sensorimotor transformation whereby information on the location of an obstacle with respect to the body is used to initiate the gait modification.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the functional role of the recorded neurons.

claim: Animals and humans must determine their relationship to stationary and moving objects for the purposes of avoidance or interception, which is essential for survival.
source: Navigation in cluttered environments dictates that animals and humans determine their relationship to stationary and moving objects for the purposes of avoidance or interception; these behaviors are essential for survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of obstacle avoidance based on established knowledge.

claim: Gibson (1958) argued that animals could use optic flow to gauge distance and location to an obstacle, and thus modify gait to avoid it.
source: Gibson, in his seminal work (Gibson, 1958), argued that animals could use optic flow to gauge distance and location to an obstacle, and thus modify gait to avoid it.
evidence: This references prior work by Gibson on optic flow.

claim: Several studies have confirmed that animals can use optic flow to gauge distance and location to an obstacle.
source: Several studies have since confirmed this premise (Prokop et al., 1997; Sun et al., 1992; Warren et al., 2001).
evidence: This references multiple studies that support Gibson's premise.

claim: Lee (1976) suggested that the brain extracts information about the time-to-contact (TTC) with an object from optic flow, a variable he called tau.
source: Later, Lee (1976) suggested that the brain extracts information about the time-to-contact (TTC) with an object from optic flow, a variable he called tau, and that this could be used to control gait.
evidence: This references Lee's work on tau and time-to-contact.

claim: Multiple studies on locomotion support the theory that tau can be used to control gait.
source: Again, multiple studies on locomotion (Shankar and Ellard, 2000; Sun et al., 1992) and other movements involving interception of moving targets (Merchant et al., 2004; Merchant and Georgopoulos, 2006) support this theory.
evidence: This references studies supporting Lee's tau theory.

claim: Tau is only one of several variables available to the brain to avoid an obstacle; distance and other time-related optical variables may also contribute.
source: However, it is important to note that tau is only one of several variables available to the brain to avoid an obstacle; distance and other time-related optical variables may also contribute (Sun and Frost, 1998; Tresilian, 1999).
evidence: This references work suggesting multiple variables contribute to obstacle avoidance.

claim: Neurons in invertebrates can process optic flow for motor activities such as flight control, distance travelled, and landing.
source: In agreement with these behavioral studies, there is evidence from invertebrates to suggest that neurons can process optic flow for motor activities such as flight control, distance travelled, and landing (Baird et al., 2013; Egelhaaf and Kern, 2002; Fotowat and Gabbiani, 2011; Srinivasan and Zhang, 2004).
evidence: This references studies on optic flow processing in invertebrates.

claim: The pigeon has neurons in the nucleus rotundus that can extract optic flow and other variables, such as tau, from visual stimuli.
source: Similarly, the pigeon has neurons in the nucleus rotundus that can extract optic flow and other variables, such as tau, from visual stimuli and which could be used for object avoidance (Sun and Frost, 1998; Wang and Frost, 1992).
evidence: This references studies on optic flow processing in pigeons.

claim: Multiple cortical structures in mammals analyze optic flow, including the middle temporal (MT/V5) and medial superior temporal (MST) cortices.
source: In mammals, multiple cortical structures analyze optic flow, including the middle temporal (MT/V5) and medial superior temporal (MST) cortices (Duffy and Wurtz, 1995, 1997; Orban, 2008), as well as the PPC, the premotor cortex, and even the motor cortex (Merchant et al., 2001, 2003; Schaafsma and Duysens, 1996; Siegel and Read, 1997).
evidence: This references studies on optic flow processing in mammalian cortex.

claim: The PPC, premotor cortex, and motor cortex in mammals analyze optic flow.
source: In mammals, multiple cortical structures analyze optic flow, including the middle temporal (MT/V5) and medial superior temporal (MST) cortices (Duffy and Wurtz, 1995, 1997; Orban, 2008), as well as the PPC, the premotor cortex, and even the motor cortex (Merchant et al., 2001, 2003; Schaafsma and Duysens, 1996; Siegel and Read, 1997).
evidence: This references studies on optic flow processing in mammalian cortex.

claim: The question of how the mammalian nervous system uses optic flow information to guide movement has been studied in only a few behaviors.
source: However, the important question of how the mammalian nervous system uses optic flow information to guide movement has been studied in only a few behaviors (Merchant and Georgopoulos, 2006), and then only for arm movements.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Previous work demonstrates the presence of neuronal activity in the PPC that begins several steps before the step over the obstacle and could contribute to planning.
source: Our previous work demonstrates the presence of neuronal activity in the PPC that begins several steps before the step over the obstacle and that could contribute to planning (Andujar et al., 2010; Drew and Marigold, 2015; Marigold et al., 2011).
evidence: This references the authors' prior work on PPC activity during obstacle avoidance.

claim: Cats performed the obstacle avoidance task in a relatively stereotypical manner.
source: The cats performed the task in a relatively stereotypical manner (Lajoie and Drew, 2007).
evidence: This describes the behavioral consistency of the task performance.

claim: Measurements of the DTC and of the TTC with the obstacle both decreased monotonically to a value of ~0 at the onset of the step over the obstacle.
source: Measurements of the DTC and of the TTC with the obstacle both decreased monotonically to a value of ~0 at the onset of the step over the obstacle (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the temporal relationship between DTC/TTC and the step over the obstacle, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In the matched task, the obstacle advanced toward the cat at the same speed as the treadmill belt on which the cat walked.
source: In one, the obstacle advanced toward the cat at the same speed as the treadmill belt on which the cat walked (matched task) while in the other, the obstacle advanced at a slower speed (visual dissociation task: Drew et al., 2008; Lajoie and Drew, 2007).
evidence: This describes the matched task condition.

claim: In the visual dissociation task, the obstacle advanced at a slower speed than the treadmill belt.
source: In one, the obstacle advanced toward the cat at the same speed as the treadmill belt on which the cat walked (matched task) while in the other, the obstacle advanced at a slower speed (visual dissociation task: Drew et al., 2008; Lajoie and Drew, 2007).
evidence: This describes the visual dissociation task condition.

claim: The speed of the treadmill on which the cat walked was 0.45 m.s−1 in these experiments.
source: As the speed of the treadmill on which the cat walked was the same in both tasks (0.45 m.s−1 in these experiments), DTC and TTC are a function of the speed of the advancing obstacle (Figure 1B).
evidence: This specifies the treadmill speed used in the experiments.

claim: In the visual dissociation task, the obstacle speed was slowed to 0.3 m.s−1.
source: However, in the visual dissociation task (obstacle speed slowed to 0.3 m.s−1), when DTC = 45 ms, TTC = 1500 ms.
evidence: This specifies the obstacle speed in the visual dissociation task.

claim: A cell in which the onset of activity is determined by TTC will discharge at the same time relative to the onset of the step over the obstacle in both the matched and the visual dissociation tasks.
source: In brief, a cell in which the onset of activity is determined by TTC will discharge at the same time relative to the onset of the step over the obstacle in both the matched and the visual dissociation tasks (red vertical line at 1000 ms in Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This describes the expected behavior of TTC-related cells, illustrated in Figure 1C,D.

claim: During the visual dissociation task, a cell related to DTC would discharge relatively earlier, indicative of the longer time required to cover the fixed distance.
source: In contrast, during the visual dissociation task, a cell related to DTC would discharge relatively earlier, indicative of the longer time required to cover the fixed distance (green vertical line at 45 cm in Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This describes the expected behavior of DTC-related cells, illustrated in Figure 1C,D.

claim: The present report is based on 67 cells recorded from two cats (37 from cat PCM7 and 30 from PCM9).
source: The present report is based on 67 cells recorded from two cats (37 from cat PCM7 and 30 from PCM9), selected from a much larger database on the basis of the criteria provided in the Materials and methods.
evidence: This specifies the size and composition of the neuronal database.

claim: Neurons were primarily recorded from the posterior bank of the ansate sulcus, the adjoining lateral bank of the lateral sulcus and the adjacent gyrus between these two sulci, corresponding to area 5b of the PPC.
source: These neurons were primarily recorded from the posterior bank of the ansate sulcus, the adjoining lateral bank of the lateral sulcus and the adjacent gyrus between these two sulci, corresponding to area 5b of the PPC; some cells were also recorded from the border region of area 5/7 (see Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of the recorded neurons, shown in Figure 2.

claim: Some cells were recorded from the border region of area 5/7.
source: These neurons were primarily recorded from the posterior bank of the ansate sulcus, the adjoining lateral bank of the lateral sulcus and the adjacent gyrus between these two sulci, corresponding to area 5b of the PPC; some cells were also recorded from the border region of area 5/7 (see Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the anatomical location of some recorded neurons, shown in Figure 2.

claim: All cells were recorded from the right PPC.
source: Note that we recorded all cells from the right PPC and that the left limb is therefore contralateral to the recording site.
evidence: This specifies the hemisphere from which recordings were made.

claim: 42 of the 67 cells were included in a previous report.
source: Some of these cells (42/67) were included in a previous report (Marigold and Drew, 2011).
evidence: This indicates overlap with a prior publication.

claim: The example cell showed a distinct increase in discharge in the two steps before the obstacle both in the left limb leads condition and in the right limb leads condition.
source: In this example, cell discharge was low and tonic during unobstructed locomotion (blue traces) and then showed a distinct increase in discharge in the two steps before the obstacle both in the left limb leads condition and in the right limb leads condition.
evidence: This describes the discharge pattern of the example cell shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increase in cell discharge began 514 ± 124 ms before the step over the obstacle in the left lead condition of the matched task.
source: The increase in cell discharge, as calculated from the average of the onsets in the individual trials (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), began 514 ± 124 ms before the step over the obstacle in the left lead condition of the matched task and 511 ± 231 ms in the right lead condition of the same task (red vertical lines).
evidence: This provides quantitative timing data for the example cell in the matched task.

claim: The increase in cell discharge began 511 ± 231 ms before the step over the obstacle in the right lead condition of the matched task.
source: The increase in cell discharge, as calculated from the average of the onsets in the individual trials (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1), began 514 ± 124 ms before the step over the obstacle in the left lead condition of the matched task and 511 ± 231 ms in the right lead condition of the same task (red vertical lines).
evidence: This provides quantitative timing data for the example cell in the matched task.

claim: In the visual dissociation task, the increase in cell discharge began 745 ± 161 ms before the step over the obstacle in the left lead condition.
source: In the visual dissociation task, the respective values were 745 ± 161 ms and 723 ± 187 ms (green vertical lines).
evidence: This provides quantitative timing data for the example cell in the visual dissociation task.

claim: In the visual dissociation task, the increase in cell discharge began 723 ± 187 ms before the step over the obstacle in the right lead condition.
source: In the visual dissociation task, the respective values were 745 ± 161 ms and 723 ± 187 ms (green vertical lines).
evidence: This provides quantitative timing data for the example cell in the visual dissociation task.

claim: A t-test showed a significant difference in the time of the onset of cell discharge between the matched and visual dissociation task for the left limb leads condition (p<0.001).
source: A t-test showed a significant difference in the time of the onset of cell discharge between the matched and visual dissociation task, both for the left limb leads condition (p<0.001) and for the right limb leads condition (p=0.002).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the difference in cell onset timing between tasks.

claim: A t-test showed a significant difference in the time of the onset of cell discharge between the matched and visual dissociation task for the right limb leads condition (p=0.002).
source: A t-test showed a significant difference in the time of the onset of cell discharge between the matched and visual dissociation task, both for the left limb leads condition (p<0.001) and for the right limb leads condition (p=0.002).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the difference in cell onset timing between tasks.

claim: The activity pattern illustrated in Figure 3 is compatible with the hypothesis that DTC determined the onset of the discharge activity.
source: The activity pattern illustrated in Figure 3 is compatible with the hypothesis that DTC determined the onset of the discharge activity (see Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This interprets the example cell as DTC-related based on its discharge pattern.

claim: There is no relationship between the onset of cell discharge and the onset of the activity in the coBr muscle in the step before the obstacle.
source: As shown in Figure 3D (left), there is no relationship between the onset of cell discharge and the onset of the activity in the coBr muscle in the step before the obstacle (a and c in Figure 3C).
evidence: This demonstrates that the cell is not simply step-related, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A significant relationship exists between the time of the end of cell discharge and the onset of activity in the flexor muscle of the lead limb during the step over the obstacle.
source: In contrast, we found a significant relationship between the time of the end of cell discharge and the onset of activity in the flexor muscle of the lead limb during the step over the obstacle (Figure 3D right) as would be expected for a limb-independent cell (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This demonstrates a temporal relationship between cell discharge and the gait modification, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Similar relationships to those illustrated in Figure 3D were observed in all cells in the database.
source: We observed similar relationships to those illustrated in Figure 3D in all cells in our database.
evidence: This generalizes the findings from the example cell to the entire population.

claim: A one-way ANOVA demonstrated a significant effect for TTC on the onset of cell discharge for the example DTC-related cell.
source: We quantified this relationship with a one-way ANOVA across the four situations, which demonstrated a significant effect for TTC (Figure 4B bottom).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that TTC varied for the DTC-related cell, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Post-hoc t-tests with Bonferroni corrections showed significant differences with task (matched versus visual dissociation) but no significant differences with condition (left or right lead) for TTC in the example DTC-related cell.
source: Post-hoc t-tests with Bonferroni corrections showed significant differences with task (matched versus visual dissociation) but no significant differences with condition (left or right lead).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for task-dependent but not limb-dependent variation in TTC for the DTC-related cell.

claim: The ANOVA showed a non-significant effect with DTC for the example DTC-related cell.
source: In contrast, the ANOVA showed a non-significant effect with DTC (Figure 4B, top), effectively indicating that the onset of cell discharge occurred when the obstacle was a constant distance from the cat, regardless of task or lead limb.
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that DTC remained constant for the DTC-related cell, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For the example TTC-related cell, a significant effect of DTC on the onset of cell discharge was found.
source: In this case, we found a significant effect of DTC (Figure 4D, top) on the onset of cell discharge.
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that DTC varied for the TTC-related cell, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Post hoc t-tests showed significant differences between the matched right lead situation and both conditions in the visual dissociation task for DTC in the example TTC-related cell.
source: Post hoc t-tests showed significant differences (asterisks) between the matched right lead situation and both conditions in the visual dissociation task.
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for task-dependent variation in DTC for the TTC-related cell.

claim: No significant effect of TTC on cell discharge was found for the example TTC-related cell.
source: However, we found no significant effect of TTC on cell discharge (Figure 4D, bottom), indicating that the onset of cell discharge occurred when the obstacle was a constant TTC regardless of task or condition.
evidence: This provides statistical evidence that TTC remained constant for the TTC-related cell, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Two populations of cells related to gap closure were identified: one group in which the onset of discharge activity occurred at a constant DTC, and a second group in which the onset of discharge occurred at a constant TTC.
source: Overall, we identified two populations of cells related to gap closure: one group in which the onset of discharge activity occurred at a constant DTC, and a second group in which the onset of discharge occurred at a constant TTC.
evidence: This summarizes the main finding of two distinct neuronal populations.

claim: 51 of 67 cells were recorded in all four situations (matched and visual dissociation task, left and right lead) and the onset of discharge activity could be measured from individual trials.
source: Figure 5 summarizes the results of the ANOVAs calculated from a population of 51/67 cells that we recorded in all four situations (matched and visual dissociation task, left and right lead) and for which we could measure the onset of the period of discharge activity from individual trials during the step over the obstacle (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This specifies the subset of cells used for the population analysis in Figure 5.

claim: 14 of 51 cells fulfilled the criterion for DTC-related cells (cell discharge varied significantly with respect to TTC but non-significantly with respect to DTC).
source: To identify DTC-related cells, we determined those cells—similar to the example in Figure 4A—in which cell discharge varied significantly with respect to TTC (p<0.01) but non-significantly with respect to DTC (p>0.01). A total of 14/51 cells fulfilled this criterion.
evidence: This quantifies the number of DTC-related cells identified in the population.

claim: 15 of 51 cells fulfilled the criterion for TTC-related cells (cell discharge varied significantly with respect to DTC but non-significantly with respect to TTC).
source: A further 15/51 cells fulfilled the inverse criterion (red traces in Figure 5B and red square in Figure 5C) and are identified as TTC-related cells.
evidence: This quantifies the number of TTC-related cells identified in the population.

claim: 6 of 51 cells showed significant effects (p<0.01) of both distance and time.
source: A further 6/51 cells showed significant effects (p<0.01) of both distance and time (green lines in Figure 5A,B left plots and green square in Figure 5C) and 16/51 cells showed non-significant effects of both time and distance (gray lines in Figure 5A,B, middle and right, and gray square in Figure 5C).
evidence: This quantifies cells showing mixed relationships to both DTC and TTC.

claim: 16 of 51 cells showed non-significant effects of both time and distance.
source: A further 6/51 cells showed significant effects (p<0.01) of both distance and time (green lines in Figure 5A,B left plots and green square in Figure 5C) and 16/51 cells showed non-significant effects of both time and distance (gray lines in Figure 5A,B, middle and right, and gray square in Figure 5C).
evidence: This quantifies cells showing no significant relationship to either DTC or TTC.

claim: Cells defined as DTC- and TTC-related were found throughout the explored region of area 5b of the PPC as well as in the border area between areas 5 and 7.
source: As indicated in Figure 2, cells defined as DTC- and TTC-related were found throughout the explored region of area 5b of the PPC as well as in the border area between areas 5 and 7.
evidence: This describes the anatomical distribution of the two cell types, shown in Figure 2.

claim: No clustering of DTC- and TTC-related cell categories was observed.
source: No clustering of categories was observed.
evidence: This indicates that the two cell types are anatomically intermixed.

claim: Cells of both categories (DTC and TTC) were recorded from each cat.
source: Cells of both categories were recorded from each cat (9 TTC-related cells from cat PCM7 and 6 from cat PCM9; 6 DTC-related cells from cat PCM7 and 8 from cat PCM9: see Figure 2 for distribution).
evidence: This indicates that the findings are consistent across both animals.

claim: The two populations of DTC- and TTC-related cells (with the exception of 1 cell) were clearly separated based on an index of the difference in standardized discharge rate between tasks.
source: As illustrated in Figure 5D, the two populations (with the exception of 1 cell) were clearly separated one from the other, reflecting the difference in their discharge profiles with respect to DTC and TTC.
evidence: This demonstrates that the two cell populations are distinct, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A bootstrapping exercise supports the contention that DTC- and TTC-related cells form two distinct categories.
source: A bootstrapping exercise performed on the DTC- and TTC-related cells supports our contention that such cells form two distinct categories (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This provides statistical validation of the two distinct cell populations.

claim: Most TTC-related cells began to discharge when the obstacle was between 300 and 1000 ms from the cat.
source: Of the cells showing a constant relationship to TTC across conditions and task, most began to discharge when the obstacle was between 300 and 1000 ms from the cat (Figure 5B, right and 5E, top).
evidence: This describes the temporal characteristics of TTC-related cells, shown in Figure 5B and 5E.

claim: DTC-related cells discharged when the obstacle was 20 to 40 cm away from the cat.
source: The cells related to DTC discharged when the obstacle was 20 to 40 cm away from the cat (Figure 5A, right and Figure 5E, bottom).
evidence: This describes the spatial characteristics of DTC-related cells, shown in Figure 5A and 5E.

claim: Cell onset values of 20 to 40 cm for DTC-related cells and 300 to 1000 ms for TTC-related cells are compatible with cell discharge beginning one or two steps before the step over the obstacle.
source: These values are compatible with cell discharge beginning one or two steps before the step over the obstacle.
evidence: This interprets the timing of cell discharge in relation to the behavioral task.

claim: The fact that cell onset occurred at varying DTC and TTC implies that there is a sequential activation of cells included within each of the two major populations.
source: The fact that cell onset occurred at varying DTC and TTC (Figure 5E) implies that there is a sequential activation of cells included within each of our two major populations.
evidence: This interprets the variability in cell onset as reflecting sequential activation.

claim: The staggered onset of cells, together with the progressive increase in discharge observed within individual cells, resulted in a prolonged and progressive increase in discharge activity for both the population of DTC-related cells and TTC-related cells.
source: When considering the overall discharge activity of both the population of DTC-related cells (Figure 6B,C) and of the TTC-related cells (Figure 6E,F), this staggered onset, together with the progressive increase in discharge observed within individual cells (Figures 3 and 4), resulted in a prolonged and progressive increase in discharge activity, for both left and right limb lead conditions.
evidence: This describes the population-level discharge pattern shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ramp increase in population discharge begins two to three steps before the step over the obstacle for the DTC-related population and slightly later for the TTC-related population.
source: This ramp increase begins two to three steps before the step over the obstacle for the DTC-related population and slightly later for the TTC-related population.
evidence: This describes the timing of the population discharge ramp.

claim: The onset of the increase in activity occurs earlier in the visual dissociation task than in the matched task for the DTC-related cells.
source: Moreover, as expected on the basis of the individual examples, the onset of this increase in activity occurs earlier in the visual dissociation task (green traces) than in the matched task (red traces) for the DTC-related cells, but at the same time for the population of TTC-related cells.
evidence: This describes the task-dependent difference in population discharge onset for DTC-related cells.

claim: The onset of the increase in activity occurs at the same time in both tasks for the population of TTC-related cells.
source: Moreover, as expected on the basis of the individual examples, the onset of this increase in activity occurs earlier in the visual dissociation task (green traces) than in the matched task (red traces) for the DTC-related cells, but at the same time for the population of TTC-related cells.
evidence: This describes the task-independent timing of population discharge onset for TTC-related cells.

claim: The peak of the discharge activity, for both populations, occurs just before or after the onset of the gait modification.
source: The peak of the discharge activity, for both populations, occurs just before or after the onset of the gait modification.
evidence: This describes the timing of peak population discharge relative to the behavioral event.

claim: The onset of the change in activity in the DTC-related population activity in the visual dissociation condition begins five to six steps before the step over the obstacle.
source: It is also noticeable in Figure 6B,C that the onset of the change in activity in the DTC-related population activity in the visual dissociation condition actually begins five to six steps before the step over the obstacle, well before the more prominent burst of activity on which we concentrate.
evidence: This describes an early increase in DTC-related population discharge in the visual dissociation task, shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: The early increase in DTC-related population discharge in the visual dissociation task represents a propensity for some of this population of cells to show a more tonic increase.
source: This early increase in discharge is not simply an effect of smearing but represents a propensity for some of this population of cells to show a more tonic increase in the visual dissociation task (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This interprets the early discharge increase as a real phenomenon rather than an artifact.

claim: One of the major effects of the acceleration was to decrease the time taken to close the gap between the cat and the obstacle for a given DTC or TTC.
source: One of the major effects of the acceleration was to decrease the time taken to close the gap between the cat and the obstacle for a given DTC or TTC.
evidence: This describes the effect of obstacle acceleration on gap closure dynamics.

claim: The acceleration produced major changes in the organization of the sequence of steps prior to the step over the obstacle.
source: This acceleration, which we always applied during the visual dissociation task, produced major changes in the organization of the sequence of steps prior to the step over the obstacle, as illustrated in Figure 7A,B.
evidence: This describes the behavioral effect of obstacle acceleration, shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: In all cases, the acceleration produced a change in the sequence of steps such that the limb that stepped over the obstacle was the opposite of that predicted on the basis of the unperturbed sequence.
source: In particular, in all cases, the acceleration produced a change in the sequence of steps such that the limb that stepped over the obstacle was the opposite of that predicted on the basis of the unperturbed sequence.
evidence: This describes the consistent effect of acceleration on limb selection.

claim: For the example DTC-related cell, cell discharge in the unperturbed visual dissociation task began 745 ms before the step over the obstacle and at a DTC of 30.6 cm.
source: In the example illustrated in Figure 7C (same DTC-related cell as in Figure 3), cell discharge in the unperturbed visual dissociation task (green trace) began 745 ms before the step over the obstacle and at a DTC of 30.6 cm.
evidence: This provides quantitative data for the example cell in the unperturbed condition.

claim: In the acceleration task, the acceleration was applied when the obstacle was 39.4 cm from the cat.
source: In the acceleration task, we applied the acceleration in step −3 of the coBr (orange box), when the obstacle was 39.4 cm from the cat.
evidence: This specifies the distance at which acceleration was applied.

claim: As the obstacle accelerated toward the cat, the example DTC-related cell started to discharge at a DTC of 30.2 cm.
source: As the obstacle accelerated toward the cat, the cell started to discharge at a DTC of 30.2 cm.
evidence: This shows that the DTC-related cell maintained a constant DTC during acceleration.

claim: Because of the acceleration, the example DTC-related cell discharge occurred only 403 ms before the cat stepped over the obstacle.
source: However, because of the acceleration, this discharge occurred only 403 ms before the cat stepped over the obstacle, resulting in the relative delay of the onset of cell discharge in the acceleration task (purple trace) compared to the visual dissociation task (see Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This shows that the time to step over changed due to acceleration while DTC remained constant.

claim: The projection of the average cell onset in the three tasks onto the DTC traces confirms that the discharge in all three tasks occurred at the same DTC for the example DTC-related cell.
source: However, the projection of the average cell onset in the three tasks (vertical lines) onto the DTC traces confirms that the discharge in all three tasks occurred at the same DTC (see values at top left of Figure 7C: DTC).
evidence: This confirms the DTC-related nature of the example cell across all tasks.

claim: The projection of the average cell onset onto the TTC trace shows that cell onset varied between the three tasks for the example DTC-related cell.
source: In contrast, the projection onto the TTC trace shows that cell onset varied between the three tasks.
evidence: This confirms that TTC varied for the DTC-related cell across tasks.

claim: The constant relationship with DTC for the example neuron held also for the 2R acceleration condition.
source: The constant relationship with DTC for this neuron held also for the 2R acceleration condition as illustrated in Figure 7D.
evidence: This shows that the DTC relationship is maintained across different acceleration conditions.

claim: An acceleration occurring prior to the predicted time of onset and the predicted DTC did not modify the onset of the cell discharge for the example DTC-related cell.
source: Therefore, an acceleration occurring prior to the predicted time of onset and the predicted DTC did not modify the onset of the cell discharge.
evidence: This shows that early accelerations do not affect DTC-related cell discharge onset.

claim: Most cells displayed similar changes in activity to those illustrated in Figure 7 in response to acceleration of the obstacle.
source: Most cells displayed similar changes in activity to those illustrated in Figure 7 in response to acceleration of the obstacle.
evidence: This generalizes the acceleration response to the broader cell population.

claim: The onset of cell discharge during the 1L condition of the acceleration task was delayed with respect to onset during the visual dissociation task for the vast majority (33/36) of cells tested.
source: The onset of cell discharge during the 1L condition of the acceleration task was delayed with respect to onset during the visual dissociation task for the vast majority (33/36) of cells tested in this condition (Figure 8D).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of 1L acceleration on cell discharge onset, shown in Figure 8D.

claim: A significant delay in cell onset was found in 19/36 cells during the 1L acceleration condition.
source: We found a significant delay in 19/36 of these cells (t-tests, p<0.05).
evidence: This provides statistical evidence for the delay in cell onset during 1L acceleration.

claim: Cell onset was relatively delayed for most (8/9) cells following acceleration in the 1R condition.
source: Cell onset was also relatively delayed for most (8/9) cells following acceleration in the 1R condition and was significant in 2/9 cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of 1R acceleration on cell discharge onset.

claim: The onset of discharge activity was less frequently delayed in the 2L and the 2R conditions, with significant differences in only 1/9 and 2/26 cells, respectively.
source: However, the onset of discharge activity was less frequently delayed in the 2L and the 2R conditions, in which we found significant differences in only 1/9 and 2/26 cells, respectively (Figure 8E).
evidence: This quantifies the effect of 2L and 2R accelerations on cell discharge onset, shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Acceleration was less likely to modify the onset of cell discharge the earlier it was applied.
source: In general, acceleration was less likely to modify the onset of cell discharge the earlier we applied it.
evidence: This summarizes the relationship between acceleration timing and its effect on cell discharge.

claim: In the majority of cases, the onset of cell discharge maintained a constant relationship to either distance or time when accelerations were included in the analysis.
source: We found that in the majority of cases, the onset of cell discharge maintained a constant relationship to either distance (e.g. Figure 5A) or time (e.g. Figure 5B).
evidence: This shows that the DTC/TTC relationships are robust to acceleration perturbations.

claim: For 8 of 14 cells showing a relationship to DTC, 20 acceleration conditions could be tested, and in most of these (18/20), the relationship with DTC was maintained during the different acceleration conditions.
source: We could test 20 acceleration conditions for 8/14 cells showing a relationship to DTC, and in most of these (18/20), the relationship with DTC was maintained during the different acceleration conditions (7/9, 1L; 2/2, 1R; 3/3, 2L; 6/6, 2R).
evidence: This quantifies how well DTC-related cells maintained their relationship during accelerations.

claim: For 8 of 15 cells with a constant relationship to TTC, 25 acceleration conditions were tested, and most (16/25) maintained this relationship with the accelerations.
source: Similarly, we tested 25 acceleration conditions for 8/15 cells with a constant relationship to TTC and most (16/25) equally maintained this relationship with the accelerations (6/11, 1L; 5/5, 1R; 1/1, 2L; 4/8, 2R).
evidence: This quantifies how well TTC-related cells maintained their relationship during accelerations.

claim: Most cells showed a marked increase in the slope of the increase in discharge frequency during the acceleration, particularly during the 1L condition.
source: Importantly, most cells showed a marked increase in the slope of the increase in discharge frequency during the acceleration, particularly during the 1L condition (Figure 8F).
evidence: This describes a key change in cell discharge dynamics during acceleration, shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Three quarters of the examples (49/67, 73%) showed an increase in the slope of the activity during the acceleration.
source: Altogether, three quarters of our examples (49/67, 73%) showed an increase in the slope of the activity during the acceleration.
evidence: This quantifies the prevalence of increased discharge slope during acceleration.

claim: The largest changes in slope were observed in the 1L and 2R conditions.
source: We observed the largest changes in slope in the 1L and 2R conditions.
evidence: This identifies which acceleration conditions produced the greatest changes in discharge slope.

claim: The slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 3.3 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 1L condition.
source: These population plots show that the slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 3.3 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 1L condition and 2.9 times greater in the 2R condition.
evidence: This quantifies the increase in population discharge slope during 1L acceleration.

claim: The slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 2.9 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 2R condition.
source: These population plots show that the slope of the discharge during the acceleration was 3.3 times greater than during the unperturbed visual dissociation task for the 1L condition and 2.9 times greater in the 2R condition.
evidence: This quantifies the increase in population discharge slope during 2R acceleration.

claim: No noticeable change in the slope of the discharge was observed for the 2L condition.
source: However, we did not observe any noticeable change in the slope of the discharge for the 2L condition (see Figure 9—figure supplement 1B), in which the acceleration occurred earlier (average of 1608 ms) than the onset of discharge activity in most cells.
evidence: This describes the lack of slope change for early accelerations (2L condition).

claim: The increased slope of the discharge in conditions where acceleration relatively delayed cell onset likely provides information on the rate of change of gap closure.
source: It is probable that the increased slope of the discharge in the conditions in which the acceleration relatively delayed cell onset provides information on the rate of change of gap closure (see Discussion).
evidence: This interprets the functional significance of the increased discharge slope.

claim: The cells in the study did not discharge purely to the visual stimulus.
source: However, the cells in our study did not discharge purely to the visual stimulus, in which case they might have been expected to discharge throughout the period that the obstacle was visible (10–12 steps before the step over the obstacle).
evidence: This argues against a purely visual response interpretation of the cell discharge.

claim: The cells began to discharge only when the obstacle was at a fixed DTC or TTC from the cat.
source: Rather, they began to discharge only when the obstacle was at a fixed DTC or TTC from the cat.
evidence: This describes the tuning of cell responses to specific DTC or TTC values.

claim: Most of the cells maintained their relationship to DTC or TTC even when the obstacle was accelerated toward the cat.
source: Moreover, most of the cells maintained this relationship even when we accelerated the obstacle toward the cat.
evidence: This demonstrates the robustness of the DTC/TTC relationships.

claim: The cells are tuned to respond to objects only when they are within a limited range of DTC or TTC.
source: This suggests that these cells are tuned to respond to objects only when they are within a limited range of DTC or TTC.
evidence: This interprets the selectivity of cell responses.

claim: A similar tuning of cell responses to distance in response to looming stimuli is found in the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) of the PPC in non-human primates.
source: A similar tuning of cell responses to distance in response to looming stimuli is found in the ventral intraparietal area (VIP) of the PPC in non-human primates (Colby et al., 1993; Graziano and Cooke, 2006; see also Hadjidimitrakis et al., 2015), as well as in the premotor cortex (PMC, Graziano et al., 1997).
evidence: This references similar findings in primate studies.

claim: Graziano has proposed that cells tuned to distance may play a role in defensive and avoidance behavior.
source: Graziano (Graziano and Cooke, 2006) has proposed that such cells may play a role in defensive and avoidance behavior.
evidence: This references a proposed functional role for distance-tuned cells.

claim: The discharge activity should be considered in the context of a coordinated and planned motor activity rather than simply in terms of the visual stimulus.
source: The discharge activity should therefore not be considered simply in terms of the visual stimulus but rather in the context of a coordinated and planned motor activity.
evidence: This proposes an interpretation of the cell discharge as motor-related rather than purely sensory.

claim: Cells responding at fixed DTC and TTC might be considered as providing important context-dependent information that is used to plan the upcoming gait modification.
source: In this respect, cells responding at fixed DTC and TTC might be considered as providing important context-dependent information that is used to plan the upcoming gait modification.
evidence: This proposes a functional role for the DTC and TTC cells in motor planning.

claim: The cells discharged in a staggered manner over a limited range of DTC and TTC.
source: Moreover, as in the experiments referenced above with respect to the VIP and PMC, the cells in our study discharged in a staggered manner over a limited range of DTC and TTC.
evidence: This describes the temporal pattern of cell activation across the population.

claim: The staggered discharge feature would provide a means for animals to continually monitor the rate of gap closure over the range in which a gait modification needs to be planned.
source: We believe that this feature of the discharge activity would provide a means for animals to continually monitor the rate of gap closure over the range in which a gait modification needs to be planned.
evidence: This proposes a functional interpretation of the staggered discharge pattern.

claim: The ability to continually monitor obstacle location over time would facilitate the detection of any non-linearities in the rate of gap closure.
source: The ability to continually monitor obstacle location over time would facilitate the detection of any non-linearities in the rate of gap closure and might be particularly important in helping the cats negotiate the obstacle when it is accelerated.
evidence: This proposes a functional advantage of continuous monitoring.

claim: In a more natural situation, the sequential activation of both DTC and TTC-related cells would be necessary for estimating the gap with a prey moving at unpredictable speeds.
source: In a more natural situation, the sequential activation of both DTC and TTC-related cells would be necessary for estimating the gap with a prey moving at unpredictable speeds, different from those of the predator.
evidence: This proposes an ecological function for the two cell populations.

claim: Although the cells discharged at fixed DTC/TTC before the gait modification, cell discharge continued until the step over the obstacle.
source: It is important to emphasize that although the cells discharged at fixed DTC/TTC before the gait modification, cell discharge continued until the step over the obstacle.
evidence: This describes the sustained nature of cell discharge.

claim: The increased discharge prior to the step over the obstacle is not a pure visual response but rather represents the starting point of a complex sensorimotor transformation involved in planning the gait modification.
source: As such, we believe that the increased discharge prior to the step over the obstacle is not a pure visual response but rather represents the starting point of a complex sensorimotor transformation involved in planning the gait modification.
evidence: This proposes an interpretation of the cell discharge as part of sensorimotor transformation.

claim: Visual input is essential for initiating the sensorimotor transformation, but once initiated planning can continue in the absence of continual visual input.
source: In this view, visual input is essential for initiating the sensorimotor transformation, but once initiated planning can continue in the absence of continual visual input.
evidence: This proposes a model for how visual information is used in motor planning.

claim: Lesion of the PPC region results in a marked locomotor deficit defined by an inability to appropriately place the plant limb in front of the obstacle.
source: Lesion of the PPC region in which we recorded these cells results in a marked locomotor deficit defined by an inability to appropriately place the plant limb in front of the obstacle (Lajoie and Drew, 2007).
evidence: This references lesion study results supporting a functional role for the PPC.

claim: The deficit from PPC lesions is indicative of an error in planning rather than one of perception or action.
source: We have previously discussed the reasons that we believe that this deficit is indicative of an error in planning rather than one of perception or action.
evidence: This interprets the nature of the deficit from PPC lesions.

claim: In the absence of information about the relative location of the obstacle and of the rate of gap closure provided by the cells in the PPC, the cat is unable to determine where to position its leg in front of the obstacle and when to start the gait modification.
source: We propose that in the absence of information about the relative location of the obstacle and of the rate of gap closure provided by the cells in the PPC, the cat is unable to determine where to position its leg in front of the obstacle and when to start the gait modification.
evidence: This proposes a functional interpretation of the lesion deficit.

claim: The ensemble activity of the population of cells demonstrates a progressive increase in discharge rate up to the time of the gait modification.
source: The ensemble activity of the population of cells demonstrates a progressive increase in discharge rate up to the time of the gait modification.
evidence: This describes the population-level discharge pattern.

claim: A similar ramp increase in cell discharge as TTC progressively decreases has been observed in the motor cortex in monkeys trained to intercept a simulated object with their arm.
source: A similar ramp increase in cell discharge as TTC progressively decreases has been observed in the motor cortex in monkeys trained to intercept a simulated object with their arm (Merchant and Georgopoulos, 2006).
evidence: This references similar findings in primate motor cortex.

claim: The ramp increase in the population discharge provides a signal that indicates the imminent requirement to make the gait modification.
source: In our task, we propose that this ramp increase in the population discharge provides a signal that indicates the imminent requirement to make the gait modification.
evidence: This proposes a functional interpretation of the ramp discharge.

claim: The ramp discharge is reminiscent of that observed in several structures and in many tasks in which motor activity is self-initiated.
source: This ramp discharge is reminiscent of that observed in several structures and in many tasks in which motor activity is self-initiated (Lebedev et al., 2008; Maimon and Assad, 2006a, 2006b; Merchant and Georgopoulos, 2006) and is particularly prevalent in tasks in which a decision to move on the basis of ambiguous or delayed information is required (Cisek and Kalaska, 2005; Cisek and Kalaska, 2010; Roitman and Shadlen, 2002; Thura and Cisek, 2014).
evidence: This references similar ramp discharge patterns in other contexts.

claim: Thura and Cisek (2014) refer to the time at which a decision is made as the time of commitment.
source: Thura and Cisek (2014) refer to the time at which such a decision is made as the time of commitment.
evidence: This references a concept from decision-making literature.

claim: The peak of activity in the population of cells indicates a time of commitment, at which point the cat initiates the gait modification.
source: We consider that the peak of activity in our population of cells also indicates a time of commitment, at which point the cat initiates the gait modification.
evidence: This proposes an interpretation of the peak discharge as a commitment signal.

claim: When the obstacle was accelerated, a greater slope of the activity was found between the onset of cell discharge and the onset of the gait modification than in the absence of acceleration.
source: In this respect, it is pertinent that when we accelerated the obstacle, we found a greater slope of the activity between the onset of cell discharge and the onset of the gait modification than in the absence of acceleration.
evidence: This describes a key finding about discharge dynamics during acceleration.

claim: The increased slope during acceleration allowed the cells to reach a similar peak value in the shorter time available to the cat to make the gait modification.
source: This increased slope allowed the cells to reach a similar peak value in the shorter time available to the cat to make the gait modification.
evidence: This interprets the functional significance of the increased slope during acceleration.

claim: The discharge is limb-independent, that is, it is identical regardless of whether the left or the right limb is the first to step over the obstacle.
source: Although we believe that the activity that we observed in this task forms part of the sensorimotor transformation that leads to the gait modification, its function has to be discussed in light of the fact that the discharge is limb-independent, that is, it is identical regardless of whether the left or the right limb is the first to step over the obstacle.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the recorded neurons.

claim: One study suggests that activity in the PPC is not expressed until the effector limb has been specified, and then only for the contralateral limb.
source: This is contrary to one study (Bernier et al., 2012) that suggests that activity in the PPC is not expressed until the effector limb has been specified, and then only for the contralateral limb (although see Chang et al., 2008)
evidence: This references a contrasting finding from another study.

claim: The nature of the task requirements is probably the main determinant of whether PPC activity is limb-dependent or limb-independent.
source: While this disparity could relate to species or area-specific differences, we believe that the nature of the task requirements is probably the main determinant.
evidence: This proposes an explanation for differences between studies.

claim: In the experiments of Bernier et al. (2012), subjects were static and an external cue specified the arm to move.
source: In the experiments of Bernier et al. (2012), subjects were static and an external cue specified the arm to move.
evidence: This describes the task conditions in a contrasting study.

claim: In the current task, the cat is walking and the leg that will step over the obstacle is not pre-defined.
source: In our task, the cat is walking and the leg that will step over the obstacle is not pre-defined.
evidence: This describes a key difference in the current task design.

claim: The decision as to which limb to use to step over the obstacle should be viewed as an emergent property of the task rather than as an instructed movement or a decision made in advance of the movement.
source: As such, we suggest that the decision as to which limb to use to step over the obstacle should be viewed as an emergent property of the task rather than as an instructed movement or a decision made in advance of the movement as in the tasks referenced above.
evidence: This proposes an interpretation of limb selection in the current task.

claim: Information on gap closure could be used to initiate a gait modification through integration with a signal that provides information on the state of the limb.
source: One possible manner in which information on gap closure could be used to initiate a gait modification is illustrated in Figure 10. In this conceptual model, we presume that there is an integration of the gap closure signal with a second signal that provides information on the state of the limb.
evidence: This proposes a conceptual model for how gap closure information is used, illustrated in Figure 10.

claim: The integration with limb state ensures that the gait modification will only be initiated when the limb is in the appropriate state.
source: The integration with limb state ensures that the gait modification will only be initiated when the limb is in the appropriate state, that is, at the end of the stance phase and ready to initiate the transfer of the limb over the obstacle.
evidence: This explains the proposed function of integrating gap closure with limb state.

claim: The integration of gap closure and limb state signals proceeds bilaterally and the limb selected to be the first to step over the obstacle depends on which side wins the competition.
source: We propose that this integration proceeds bilaterally and the limb selected to be the first to step over the obstacle depends on which side wins the competition.
evidence: This proposes a bilateral competition model for limb selection.

claim: All of the cells recorded in this study were located in layer V and therefore project to subcortical structures, including the basal ganglia and the cerebellum.
source: Although we do not wish to unduly speculate on where this integration would occur, we would note that all of the cells recorded in this study were located in layer V and therefore project to subcortical structures, including the basal ganglia and the cerebellum.
evidence: This describes the anatomical location and projection targets of the recorded neurons.

claim: The results provide new insights, at the single cell level, into the sensorimotor transformations that underlie the control of visually guided walking.
source: In conclusion, our results provide new insights, at the single cell level, into the sensorimotor transformations that underlie the control of visually guided walking.
evidence: This summarizes the contribution of the study.

claim: The demonstration of populations of cells that can serve to provide information on gap closure and potentially initiate precise gait changes is a novel contribution to understanding the control mechanisms used to guide locomotion.
source: The demonstration of populations of cells that can serve to provide information on gap closure and potentially initiate precise gait changes is a novel contribution to our understanding of the control mechanisms used to guide locomotion.
evidence: This emphasizes the novelty of the findings.

claim: The PPC may have a privileged position in contributing to the ability to plan the gait adjustments needed to negotiate a complex environment.
source: Taken together with the results from studies in various species that show a contribution of the PPC to spatial navigation (Calton and Taube, 2009; Harvey et al., 2012; Whitlock, 2014), it is possible that the PPC may have a privileged position in contributing to our ability to plan the gait adjustments needed to negotiate a complex environment.
evidence: This proposes a broader functional role for the PPC in locomotor control.

claim: Cats were trained to walk on a treadmill at a constant speed of 0.45 m.s−1.
source: We initially trained the cats to walk on a treadmill at a constant speed of 0.45 m.s−1 (unobstructed locomotion) and then trained them to step over obstacles attached to a second belt that moved at the same speed as the treadmill (matched task).
evidence: This describes the training protocol.

claim: Cats very rarely, if ever, hit the obstacle, even in conditions in which the acceleration occurred just before the planned gait modification.
source: Note that cats very rarely, if ever, hit the obstacle, even in conditions in which the acceleration occurred just before the planned gait modification.
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance of the cats.

claim: Two obstacles (cylindrical in shape and each of 10 cm cross-section), separated by 3 m, were attached to the treadmill belt.
source: Two obstacles (cylindrical in shape and each of 10 cm cross-section), separated by 3 m, were attached to the treadmill belt.
evidence: This describes the obstacle configuration.

claim: The cat generally made 12–14 steps (6–7 step cycles) between each obstacle.
source: Depending on the speed of the treadmill, the cat generally made 12–14 steps (6–7 step cycles) between each obstacle.
evidence: This describes the step pattern between obstacles.

claim: The obstacle became visible to the cat ~2 m before the step over the obstacle.
source: The obstacle became visible to the cat ~2 m before the step over the obstacle.
evidence: This specifies when the obstacle became visible.

claim: The obstacle was visible to the cat for 5–7 s before the gait modification, during which time the cat made 10–12 steps.
source: The obstacle was therefore visible to the cat for 5–7 s before the gait modification, during which time the cat made 10–12 steps.
evidence: This describes the duration of obstacle visibility.

claim: All handling and surgical procedures followed the recommendations of the Canadian Council for the Protection of Animals.
source: All handling and surgical procedures followed the recommendations of the Canadian Council for the Protection of Animals, and the animal ethics committee at the Université de Montréal approved the experimental protocols (#12_082).
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: A stainless steel baseplate was placed over the right PPC based on an MRI taken 1–2 weeks before the surgery.
source: In brief, based on an MRI taken 1–2 weeks before the surgery, we placed a stainless steel baseplate (internal dimensions = 12 by 6 mm) over the right PPC and then formed a recording chamber around it with dental acrylic.
evidence: This describes the surgical preparation for recordings.

claim: Pairs of Teflon-insulated, stainless steel braided wires were implanted into selected fore- and hindlimb muscles to record electromyographic (EMG) activity.
source: We implanted pairs of Teflon-insulated, stainless steel braided wires into selected fore- and hindlimb muscles to record electromyographic (EMG) activity.
evidence: This describes the EMG recording method.

claim: Microwires were inserted into the cerebral peduncle to allow for antidromic identification of projection neurons in layer V of the PPC.
source: To allow for antidromic identification of projection neurons in layer V of the PPC, we inserted microwires into the cerebral peduncle by using a harpoon assembly (Drew, 1993; Palmer, 1978).
evidence: This describes the method for identifying layer V neurons.

claim: Experiments started 1 week after the surgery.
source: Experiments started 1 week after the surgery.
evidence: This specifies the recovery period before experiments began.

claim: A conventional glass-insulated tungsten microelectrode (0.5–1.5 MΩ) was introduced into the PPC using a custom-made microdrive.
source: In each recording session, we introduced a conventional glass-insulated tungsten microelectrode (0.5–1.5 MΩ) into the PPC using a custom-made microdrive.
evidence: This describes the recording electrode and method.

claim: The electrode was advanced until stimulation of the electrodes in the cerebral peduncle produced antidromic discharges, providing evidence that the electrode had reached layer V.
source: We advanced the electrode until stimulation of the electrodes in the cerebral peduncle produced antidromic discharges either in an isolated unit or in smaller units in the background. This provided evidence that the electrode had reached layer V.
evidence: This describes the method for confirming electrode depth.

claim: Cell activity was recorded from well-isolated single units while the cat walked on the treadmill.
source: We recorded cell activity from well-isolated single units while the cat walked on the treadmill in the matched task until approximately 10 steps over the obstacle with each leg as the lead limb had been made.
evidence: This describes the recording protocol.

claim: Steps in which the obstacle accelerated were interspersed unpredictably with steps where the obstacle continued at its pre-set speed.
source: Steps in which the obstacle accelerated were interspersed unpredictably with steps where the obstacle continued at its pre-set speed.
evidence: This describes the randomization of acceleration trials.

claim: The entire data collection period occupied 15–20 min.
source: The entire data collection period occupied 15–20 min, although we sometimes lost cell stability before we could complete the recording session.
evidence: This specifies the duration of recording sessions.

claim: EMG activity was band-pass filtered at 100–475 Hz and digitized online at a frequency of 1 KHz.
source: We band-pass filtered EMG activity at 100–475 Hz and digitized it online at a frequency of 1 KHz.
evidence: This describes the EMG signal processing.

claim: Cell activity was digitized at a frequency of 100 KHz to discriminate cells offline.
source: To discriminate cells offline, we digitized cell activity at a frequency of 100 KHz.
evidence: This describes the cell recording sampling rate.

claim: A six-camera Vicon motion analysis system recorded, at 100 Hz, the position of light-reflecting points placed on a rod attached to the head of the cat and along the length of each obstacle.
source: In all experiments, a six-camera Vicon motion analysis system recorded, at 100 Hz, the position of light-reflecting points placed on a rod attached to the head of the cat and along the length of each obstacle.
evidence: This describes the motion capture system used.

claim: Single units were discriminated offline on the basis of waveform amplitude and shape.
source: We discriminated single units offline on the basis of waveform amplitude and shape.
evidence: This describes the spike sorting method.

claim: The onset and offset of activity in the left, contralateral (co) and right, ipsilateral (i) Br or ClB EMG was marked for every step during the entire locomotor sequence.
source: For sections of data with stable action potentials and with stable locomotion, we marked the onset and offset of activity in the left, contralateral (co) and right, ipsilateral (i) Br or ClB EMG for every step during the entire locomotor sequence.
evidence: This describes the EMG analysis procedure.

claim: Cell activity during unobstructed locomotion was calculated on the basis of the discharge activity five steps before the step over the obstacle, combining all tasks.
source: Cell activity during unobstructed locomotion was calculated on the basis of the discharge activity five steps before the step over the obstacle, combining all tasks.
evidence: This describes how baseline activity was calculated.

claim: Cell discharge for each trial was transformed into an instantaneous frequency (1000/interspike interval) and filtered at 50 Hz.
source: To determine the temporal relationships between cell discharge activity and different behavioral events on a trial-by-trial basis, we transformed cell discharge for each trial into an instantaneous frequency (1000/interspike interval) and filtered it at 50 Hz (fourth order Butterworth algorithm).
evidence: This describes the signal processing for cell discharge analysis.

claim: The onset of cell activity relative to the step over the obstacle was calculated for each trial as an increase or decrease of activity that exceeded 2SD of the cell discharge that occurred between 2.5 and 3 s before the step over the obstacle.
source: By using interactive software, we calculated the onset of cell activity relative to the step over the obstacle for each trial as an increase or decrease of activity that exceeded 2SD of the cell discharge that occurred between 2.5 and 3 s before the step over the obstacle (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the method for detecting cell discharge onset.

claim: The distance of the obstacle from the cat (distance-to-contact; DTC) and the time-to-contact (TTC) with the obstacle were calculated at the moment of the onset of change in cell discharge, for each individual trial.
source: We then calculated the distance of the obstacle from the cat (distance-to-contact; DTC) and the time-to-contact (TTC) with the obstacle at the moment of the onset of change in cell discharge, for each individual trial, by measuring the relative distance of the rod on the cat's head from the obstacle.
evidence: This describes how DTC and TTC were calculated.

claim: Data values that exceeded 1.5 * IQR were removed from the analysis.
source: We removed data values that exceeded 1.5 * IQR from the analysis.
evidence: This describes the outlier removal criterion.

claim: On average, outlier removal removed 2.5% of the trials.
source: On average, this removed 2.5% of the trials (we recorded an average of 62 trials/cell).
evidence: This quantifies the impact of outlier removal.

claim: Average discharge rates of cell activity (bin width = 2 ms) were calculated by synchronizing activity to the onset of the Br or ClB.
source: After removal of outliers, we calculated average discharge rates of cell activity (bin width = 2 ms) by synchronizing activity to the onset of the Br or ClB.
evidence: This describes the method for creating peri-event histograms.

claim: A change in discharge activity beginning >200 ms before the onset of activity in the Br or ClB differentiated step-advanced cells from step-related cells.
source: A change in discharge activity beginning >200 ms before the onset of activity in the Br or ClB differentiated step-advanced cells from step-related cells.
evidence: This defines the criterion for classifying step-advanced cells.

claim: A limb-independent cell was defined as one in which discharge activity ended at approximately the same time (<200 ms difference) with respect to the coBr during the left lead condition and with respect to the iBr during the right lead condition.
source: We defined a limb-independent cell as one in which discharge activity (as determined from the averaged displays) ended at approximately the same time (<200 ms difference) with respect to the coBr (coClB) during the left, contralateral forelimb, lead condition and with respect to the iBr (iClB) during the right, ipsilateral forelimb, lead condition (see Andujar et al., 2010; Marigold and Drew, 2011).
evidence: This defines the criterion for classifying limb-independent cells.

claim: One-way ANOVAs determined the effect of distance and time on the time of onset of cell discharge (significant effects determined at the alpha = 0.01 level).
source: One-way ANOVAs determined the effect of distance and time on the time of onset of cell discharge (significant effects determined at the alpha = 0.01 level).
evidence: This describes the statistical method used to identify DTC and TTC relationships.

claim: Significant differences between pairs of values using t-tests were determined using an alpha of 0.05.
source: Significant differences between pairs of values using t-tests were determined using an alpha of 0.05.
evidence: This specifies the significance threshold for t-tests.

claim: When multiple comparisons were made, a Bonferroni correction was used.
source: When multiple comparisons were made we used a Bonferroni correction.
evidence: This describes the correction for multiple comparisons.

claim: An index was calculated based on the difference in standardized discharge rate (Z score) between the visual dissociation task and the matched task.
source: To create an index of the difference in discharge with respect to DTC and TTC, we calculated the difference between the averaged standardized discharge rate (Z score) during the visual dissociation task (left + right/2) and that during the matched task (left +right/2).
evidence: This describes the method for calculating the DTC/TTC index.

claim: Cells were included in the analysis if they were located within the caudal bank of the ansate sulcus or the adjoining caudal gyrus, corresponding to area 5b and the border with area 7.
source: We included cells in the analysis on the following bases: (1) The cells were located within the caudal bank of the ansate sulcus or the adjoining caudal gyrus, corresponding to area 5b and the border with area 7.
evidence: This specifies an inclusion criterion based on anatomical location.

claim: Cells were included if they were located within cortical layer V, as determined on the basis of antidromic stimulation.
source: (2) The cells were located within cortical layer V, as determined on the basis of the antidromic stimulation (43/67 cells were antidromically activated, as determined by collision with spontaneous action potentials, and the other 24/67 cells were adjacent to identified cells).
evidence: This specifies an inclusion criterion based on cortical layer.

claim: 43 of 67 cells were antidromically activated, as determined by collision with spontaneous action potentials.
source: (2) The cells were located within cortical layer V, as determined on the basis of the antidromic stimulation (43/67 cells were antidromically activated, as determined by collision with spontaneous action potentials, and the other 24/67 cells were adjacent to identified cells).
evidence: This quantifies how many cells were antidromically identified.
